summary:
ASTRA-CARE | MICRO-G is an autonomous, edge-AI health-monitoring platform for astronauts on deep-space missions such as Artemis and Mars transit. We built an interactive software prototype, with a live demo (nasa1.html) and a six-module dashboard. It tracks heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, sleep, cumulative radiation dose and microgravity bone-mineral-density loss. It compares each astronaut’s readings against their own personal baseline and detects drift over time. It also correlates indicators, for example radiation spikes with sleep disruption, to separate sensor noise from real physiological change.

This addresses the challenge of helping astronauts monitor indicators, track changes and act on guidance without relying on Earth. With up to 20 minutes of one-way signal delay to Mars, real-time ground oversight isn’t possible. ASTRA-CARE runs entirely on local hardware and gives countermeasure recommendations, then escalates to flight surgeons when thresholds are crossed. It supports medical protocols and does not prescribe drugs. It also has terrestrial uses, including remote telemedicine, osteoporosis tracking and isolated-workforce monitoring.
details:
What it does and how it works
ASTRA-CARE | MICRO-G is a five-layer health-intelligence pipeline designed to run locally on spacecraft hardware.

  1. Data acquisition: it takes in telemetry from wearables, radiation dosimeters and ultrasound units.
  2. Edge processing: onboard AI cleans and validates the readings, so the system keeps working during communication blackouts.
  3. Health intelligence: it analyses bone-density drift, cumulative radiation dose, fluid shift and cardiovascular strain against each astronaut's personal baseline.
  4. Recommendation engine: it generates countermeasures, verification prompts and escalation steps.
  5. Interface: a color-coded dashboard with six modules: Mission Overview, Health Monitoring, Microgravity Adaptation, AI Health Assistant, Health Analytics and Mission Reports.

A guided five-step workflow takes the astronaut from detecting a change to confirming the reading, comparing it to their baseline, getting guidance and escalating to a flight surgeon if needed. In our example scenario, a solar-particle spike that coincides with disrupted sleep triggers an automatic dosimeter check and a shelter recommendation, and flags the flight surgeon.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Crew can act on health changes immediately instead of waiting up to 20 minutes for a reply from Earth.
  • Monitoring is automatic, so astronauts don't have to log data by hand.
  • Early detection of bone loss (about 1–2% per month) and radiation accumulation supports mission safety and crew performance.
  • The same design can serve remote telemedicine, osteoporosis tracking and isolated-workforce monitoring on Earth.

Tools and technologies
We built an interactive web prototype (nasa1.html) that simulates live sensor streams and the countermeasure engine, plus a 13-slide presentation. [Add the languages, libraries and tools you actually used, e.g. HTML/CSS/JavaScript, any chart or 3D library, design tools.] The sensor inputs are simulated. The architecture is designed for real wearables, dosimeters and ultrasound hardware, but we did not build physical hardware.

Creativity
It combines radiation dosimetry and microgravity bone-loss tracking in one offline decision engine. It also correlates indicators with each other instead of reading each in isolation. The "Mars time-delay fail-safe" is the core design idea.

Factors we considered

  • Autonomy during signal blackouts.
  • Personalized baselines instead of population averages.
  • A clinical safety boundary: the system supports established protocols and does not prescribe medication.
  • Telling sensor noise apart from real physiological change.
  • A clear interface for high-stress environments.
  • Future dual use on Earth.
